items.readable_text:
Content:
The power rule states that the limit of a power is the power of the limit. More precisely, if [MATH: n] is any positive integer and [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}f(x)=L,] then

Content:
[MATH: lim_(x → a)(f(x))^{n} = (lim_(x → a)f(x))^{n} = L^{n}.]

Content:
For example, with the power rule, we can evaluate a limit like [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}(3x-4)^{8}] by evaluating the limit of the expression within parentheses and then taking the power of the result.

Content:
[MATH: lim_(x → 2)(3x − 4)^{8}|= (lim_(x → 2)(3x − 4))^{8}; = (3 ⋅ 2 − 4)^{8}; = 2^{8}; = 256.]

sections.normalized_html: Find [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 1} \dfrac{\sqrt{x+8}}{x-2}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Applying the quotient rule, we get [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1} \dfrac{\sqrt{x+8}}{x-2} =\dfrac{\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1} \sqrt{x+8}}{\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}(x-2)}.] We calculate the limits of the numerator and denominator, separately.

Applying the root rule in the numerator, we have

[MATH: lim_(x → 1)sqrt(x + 8)|= sqrt(lim_(x → 1)(x + 8)); = sqrt(1 + 8); = sqrt(9); = 3.]

For the denominator, we have [MATH: lim_(x → 1)(x − 2)|= 1 − 2; = − 1.]

Consequently, [MATH: lim_(x → 1)(sqrt(x + 8))/(x − 2)|= (3)/((− 1)); = − 3.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The power rule states that the limit of a power is the power of the limit. More precisely, if [MATH: n] is any positive integer and [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}f(x)=L,] then

Content:
[MATH: lim_(x → a)(f(x))^{n} = (lim_(x → a)f(x))^{n} = L^{n}.]

Content:
For example, with the power rule, we can evaluate a limit like [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}(3x-4)^{8}] by evaluating the limit of the expression within parentheses and then taking the power of the result.

Content:
[MATH: lim_(x → 2)(3x − 4)^{8}|= (lim_(x → 2)(3x − 4))^{8}; = (3 ⋅ 2 − 4)^{8}; = 2^{8}; = 256.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Applying the Power Rule to Compute a Limit

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}\left[(2x-1)^3(x-2)^9\right].]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Here, we apply the product rule and the power rule to get

[MATH: \eqalign{
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}\left[(2x-1)^3(x-2)^9\right] &= \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}(2x-1)^3\cdot \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}(x-2)^9\[3pt]
&= \left(\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}(2x-1)\right)^3\cdot \left(\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}(x-2)\right)^9\[3pt]
&= (2\cdot 3 -1)^3\cdot (3-2)^9\[3pt]
&= 5^3 \cdot 1^9\[3pt]
& = 125.
}]

Content:
For example, with the root rule, we can evaluate a limit like [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}\sqrt{3x-2}] by evaluating the limit of the expression within the root and then taking the root of the result:

Content:
[MATH: lim_(x → 2)sqrt(3x − 2)|= sqrt(lim_(x → 2)(3x − 2)); = sqrt(3 ⋅ 2 − 2); = sqrt(4); = 2]

Item 9 — Example: Applying the Root Rule to Compute a Limit

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 1} \dfrac{\sqrt{x+8}}{x-2}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Applying the quotient rule, we get
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1} \dfrac{\sqrt{x+8}}{x-2}
=\dfrac{\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1} \sqrt{x+8}}{\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}(x-2)}.]
We calculate the limits of the numerator and denominator, separately.

Applying the root rule in the numerator, we have

[MATH: lim_(x → 1)sqrt(x + 8)|= sqrt(lim_(x → 1)(x + 8)); = sqrt(1 + 8); = sqrt(9); = 3.]

For the denominator, we have
[MATH: lim_(x → 1)(x − 2)|= 1 − 2; = − 1.]

Consequently,
[MATH: lim_(x → 1)(sqrt(x + 8))/(x − 2)|= (3)/((− 1)); = − 3.]

Item 12 — Tutorial: Combining Different Rules

Content:
If we combine the power rule and the root rule, then we get the following useful generalization: if [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}f(x)=L,] then for any fraction [MATH: p/q,] we have
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}\left(f(x)\right)^{p/q} = \left(\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a} f(x)\right)^{p/q} = L^{p/q}]

Content:
provided that [MATH: L^{p/q}] exists.

Content:
For example, we can evaluate a limit like [MATH: \lim_\limits{y\rightarrow 64} y^{-1/6}] by evaluating the limit of [MATH: y] and then exponentiating the result to the fractional exponent:

Content:
[MATH: lim_(y → 64)y^{− 1/6}|= (lim_(y → 64)y)^{− 1/6}; = (64)^{− 1/6}; = (2^{6})^{− 1/6}; = 2^{− 1}; = (1)/(2)]

Item 13 — Example: Combining Different Rules to Compute a Limit Given a Graph

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
According to the power rule and the quotient rules,

[MATH: lim_(x → − 2)((f(x))/(x^{2} − 1))^{2/3}|= ((lim_(x → − 2)f(x))/(lim_(x → − 2)(x^{2} − 1)))^{2/3}.]

We find from the graph that the limit of the numerator is

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow -2} f(x)=1.]

We also calculate the limit of the denominator as
[MATH: lim_(x → − 2)(x^{2} − 1)|= (− 2)^{2} − 1 = 3.]

So we get
[MATH: lim_(x → − 2)((f(x))/(x^{2} − 1))^{2/3}|= ((lim_(x → − 2)f(x))/(lim_(x → − 2)(x^{2} − 1)))^{2/3}; = ((1)/(3))^{2/3}; = root((1)/(9), 3).]
